The first one is the hard one

Four things you're weighing all at once.

Every other senior role, you've hired it before or you've done the job yourself. Here are the four questions that come up on almost every first call, and how we answer them.

What should this role actually be?

“Head of AI” means four different jobs depending on where your company is today. We define the mandate with you first — what has to be true in twelve months, who they report to, and which roles can wait — before anyone writes a job description.

Included in every search

How do I know who's the real thing?

Our experts have built these systems themselves, so they interview on what actually happened: what shipped, what got cancelled, what broke and who fixed it. Every finalist comes to you with a scorecard against your role — strengths, concerns and all.

Two experts on every shortlist

Are we about to overpay?

Compensation for these roles has moved fast, and a lot of the numbers in circulation come from the very top of the market. We show you what's being offered and accepted right now, so you can take a number to your board that holds up.

Live market data, not a survey

What happens after they start?

The first ninety days decide whether this works. We stay in the room — thinking through the early calls on team, tools and spend with both of you while there's still room to change course.

Ninety days past the offer

The search

We find and assess them

  • The role, defined against your business — not a template borrowed from a tech giant's careers page.
  • The market approached directly — the people leading AI in your industry, by name, because our experts work alongside them.
  • Every finalist interviewed by an AI expert who has held the job you're hiring for.
  • A scorecard, a recommendation and the concerns — plus a debrief so you can see how we got there.
The consulting

We think it through with you

  • Whether this hire is your right next step — sometimes the answer is to wait a quarter and sort out who owns the data first.
  • Build it or buy it — one central team or people embedded in each department.
  • Which problem to tackle first, and just as usefully, what to leave alone this year.
  • A seat with your peers — private sessions on what is genuinely working with AI this quarter, and what isn't.

Our experts have made every one of these calls themselves, with their own budget at stake.

Which leader you need

Your first AI hire is one of these four.

Which one depends on where you are today. Working that out together is usually the most valuable half-hour of the whole process.

A few experiments, nobody owns it Head of Applied AI

Focus the work on the few ideas with a business owner and a number attached, stop the rest, and set a baseline you can measure against. Hire them senior enough that “no” sticks.

The demos are great, nothing is live Director of AI Engineering

Take one job people do every day and get it fully live — someone's name on it, a way to switch it off, and a cost agreed up front. The point isn't the technology; it's proving you can run this day to day.

One thing works, now everyone wants it VP of Artificial Intelligence

Turn that one success into something other teams can reuse and run themselves. Half this job is technical. The other half is getting people to change how they work.

The business would notice if it stopped Chief AI Officer

Own AI the way a CFO owns money: know everything that's running, what it's exposed to, and have the authority to switch something off — then explain all of it to the board in language they already use.
